newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Visiting US congressmen urge peace in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Visiting US congressmen urge peace in N.Ireland.

text.p: A U.S. congressional delegation called during a visit to Dublin on Saturday for an end to violence in Northern Ireland and said efforts to secure peace should be stepped up on both sides of the Atlantic.

"We must redouble our efforts on both sides of the Atlantic to secure the peace that ... we all desire on this island through inclusive all party talks and we hope we can come to that point at an early date," delegation chairman Benjamin Gilman told reporters ahead of a luncheon with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton.

The 17 members of U.S. congress, on a fact-finding visit to Europe, met leaders of the main Northern Ireland political parties on Friday, including Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political arm, Sinn Fein.

"We have just come back from meetings in the North yesterday with all representatives of the many parties and have a better insight and a better understanding of the complexity of this problem," Gilman, who is chairman of the House of Representatives International Relations Committee, said.

The visit comes in the wake the murder of a British soldier, Stephen Restorick, 23, who died from a sniper's bullet in the back while on duty at an army checkpoint in the village of Bessbrook on Wednesday night.
Gilman, a New York Republican, said he hoped the "misguided returns to violence" would be short lived.
"Peace and reconciliation can only come through political means and not the use of violence and force," he said.
Bruton said on Saturday the Irish government will not enter into political consensus, fronts, or alliances of any kind with those who retain the option of violence for political ends.
He added that the conflict in Northern Ireland will not be resolved by a peace process alone but also required forgiveness on the part of the victims of violence.

"That is why the victims of Bloody Sunday must be heard," Bruton told reporters. "Only when victims have been heard, can forgiveness begin. Only when there is forgiveness can there be reconciliation...everlasting peace."
On Saturday, a light aircraft towing the message "Ceasefire Now" was preparing to fly over Dublin's Lansdowne Road Stadium just before an Ireland-England international rugby match.
The demonstration has been organised by the group Solidarity to Organise Peace in response to the killing of Lance Bombardier Restorick.
On Sunday members of the same group will lay a wreath at the gate of the British embassy in Dublin which they hope will then be sent on to the soldier's funeral.
